processing: A pan-fired strip green tea from one bud with two leaves just opening. The leaf is lightly spread, then goes through two rounds of firing and rolling before it is finished dry in the pan.
harvest_season: Picking starts in late March or early April, and the year can run to five pickings: spring, summer, high summer, autumn and winter.
appearance_dry: Tight, heavy strips of a silver-grey colour with a green cast.
appearance_liquor: Clear with a distinct green tint.
taste_profile: Smooth and brisk, with an aroma that recalls orchid, mung bean or almond and shifts with the season.

brewing.notes: General advice for pan-fired greens: water around 85 C and an open vessel. Compare aromas between spring and later pickings if you can.

vintage_note: Sales practice for this tea is little documented. As with other Fujian greens, the current year's spring picking is the one to look for, drunk within about a year; later pickings exist and are generally the cheaper leaf.
description:
Shiting Lü is a pan-fired green tea from Fengzhou in Nan'an, southern Fujian, grown around Jiuri Mountain and Lianhua Peak. It stands out as a green tea in a province better known for oolong and white tea.

The tea is known locally for its 'three greens and three aromas'. The three greens are the silver-green dry leaf, the green liquor and the tender green spent leaf. The three aromas are orchid, mung bean and almond, which are said to shift as the seasons change.

The method is plain and hands-on: the leaf is fried, rolled, fried again and rolled again before the last dry in the pan. That produces tight, weighty strips and a fuller taste than many bud-only greens.

Brew it like other pan-fired greens, with water a little off the boil and steeps that are not too long. It is mainly a regional tea, so buying it usually means going through a Fujian seller, and it is worth asking which picking you are getting.
history:
Local accounts tie the name to a stone pavilion built on Lianhua Peak in 1506, in the Ming dynasty, known as the 'Never Ageing Pavilion'. The tea reached market early in the year and was praised as the first spring tea of that pavilion.

Little else about its history is firmly documented. Today it is usually mentioned among Fujian's notable green teas.
